articles.title_orig: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.title_zh: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
articles.content_orig:
Nine American citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in occupied West Bank since 2022
The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank , including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years.
The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children.
The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor.
Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee.
“While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”
Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022, and the senators say none of the cases has resulted in accountability. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad.
Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen.
The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him.
Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it.
“If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.”
In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank.
The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025.
A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes.
Many of the Democrats , who have historically been lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years.
When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000-pound bombs.
The measures failed because every Republican voted against it.

articles.title_orig: Caleb Flynn, former ‘American Idol’ singer, found guilty of wife’s murder
articles.title_zh: Caleb Flynn, former ‘American Idol’ singer, found guilty of wife’s murder
articles.content_orig:
Former “American Idol” singer Caleb Flynn was found guilty Tuesday of murdering his wife in their Ohio home in February.
The jury took a little over two hours to convict Flynn on all nine counts of murder, assault and tampering with evidence in the death of Ashley Flynn, 37.
After Judge Jeannine Pratt read the verdict in Miami County Court of Common Pleas in Troy, Flynn broke down in tears and repeatedly wiped his nose and eyes. He was taken from the courtroom in handcuffs.
Following the proceedings, Miami County Prosecuting Attorney Paul Watkins read from a statement released by Ashley’s family, who said the verdict brings “justice and accountability.”
“However,” he continued, reading from the statement, “no verdict can bring Ashley back, give the girls back their mother, or erase the pain our family has endured. The cruelty of what happened to Ashley, and the things we’ve been forced to hear and relive, have at times felt unbearable.”
Sentencing will be Oct. 5, when Flynn faces up to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Defense attorney Patrick Mulligan said his client will challenge the verdict.
“This decision will be tested thoroughly in the Court of Appeals,” Mulligan said after Tuesday’s proceedings.
Caleb Flynn found guilty of wife's murder
Flynn, a former music pastor, told a 911 dispatcher that his wife, who worked as a schoolteacher and volleyball coach, had been shot multiple times in the head by an intruder. He told the dispatcher that he did not know whether the intruder was still in their Tipp City home.
In police interviews played in court, Flynn told officers that he was sleeping on the couch when he woke up to the sound of gunshots. He said that a day before the killing, a man had come to their home and handed his wife an American flag while making a “weird sales pitch for America.”
When police arrived at the home on the day of the shooting, the garage door, a side door and the center console of Flynn’s pickup truck were open. Flynn told police that he kept a gun in the console, but no weapon was found there.
Prosecutors alleged that Flynn, 40, staged the home invasion to mislead investigators and shared thoughts of killing his wife in text messages to his then-mistress. Authorities never found the gun used in the killing.
“The evidence has proven the defendant’s account to be a complete fabrication,” Assistant Prosecuting Attorney Matthew C. Joseph said in closings Tuesday.
“While the defendant told law enforcement that he was sleeping, his electronic devices documented something different. They documented movement and activity in the hours leading up to Ashley’s murder,” Joseph said. “The defendant said he was sleeping. His devices say he was awake and moving.”
Joseph told the court that Flynn, who sang in televised auditions in Chicago for Season 12 of “American Idol” in 2013 but did not advance to the main competition, “wanted to be a victim” and wanted to “keep his mistress and have his daughters all to himself.”
“Being the victim allowed him to do that without being the husband who left his wife for a mistress,” Joseph said. “Instead, he’d be the husband whose wife was tragically murdered by an unknown intruder.”
Over eight days, the jury heard from 40 prosecution witnesses, including Alleigha Botner, who said she met Flynn when she was 20 and an intern at his church. She said they had been having an affair at the time of Ashley’s killing.
Botner, now 24, testified that Flynn had made remarks that he hated his wife and harbored thoughts of killing her. Botner sobbed on the stand as she read some of their text messages, telling the court that she regretted having told him in one message: “I want to kill her, Caleb.”
Botner said Flynn replied: “That makes two of us.”
In other text messages shown in court, Flynn discussed wanting his wife dead.
“I was up until 4 a.m. last night crying, literally trying to think of ways to kill her and not go to jail,” he is alleged to have written in a text in August 2025, about six months before the killing.
In another text, Botner said she wasn’t serious. “I’m not asking that you take her life obviously, because that’s not what you should do, and I know you actually wouldn’t,” she wrote. “But to make the divorce happen, it would change everything.”
Botner told the court that her feelings about Flynn have since changed and that she hated him. When a prosecutor asked her why, she said: “Because I believe that he murdered his wife.”
The defense rested Monday without calling a single witness.
Mulligan, one of Flynn’s defense attorneys, said in his closing argument that being “unfaithful doesn’t equal murder.”
“This case is wholly lacking in concrete evidence. Connecting a couple of meaningless dots doesn’t solve the case,” he said.
Afterward, Mulligan said the defense was “disappointed” in the jury’s decision.
Ashley’s family said she lived a virtuous life.
“She loved being a mom,” Watkins said, still reading from the family statement. “She prayed over her girls, taught them to love God and showed them what it looked like to live with faith, kindness, joy and grace. We refuse to let the evil that ended Ashley’s life have the final word in her story.”
Watkins praised law enforcement and prosecutors for their success in prosecuting the case. He said he is tired of talking about Flynn and wants renewed focus on the victim.
“This world would be a much better place if all of us in it lived like Ashley,” he said.
Selina Guevara is an NBC News field producer, based in Chicago.
Shaquille Brewster is a correspondent for NBC News.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data center expansion
articles.title_zh: Trump, AI CEOs sign voluntary safety pact, back data center expansion
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and the leaders of the country's largest artificial intelligence companies have signed a set of voluntary safety standards, as calls mount for tighter guardrails on AI technology.
"It's almost like a constitution, in a way," Mr. Trump said while flanked by SpaceX's Elon Musk, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic's Dario Amodei, Nvidia's Jensen Huang, OpenAI's Greg Brockman, Google's Sundar Pichai and a throng of other tech executives.
Following a lunch meeting at the White House , Johnson said the group signed an accord on "super intelligence" — Mr. Trump's preferred term for AI. He described it as a "joint commitment" and "statement of principles" that will voluntarily hold the companies to "robust internal controls."
Asked if the deal was binding, Mr. Trump said: "I think it's morally binding."
"I think I'm seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police," the president later said.
The tech companies committed to "four layers of controls and audits" to ensure the AI models are acting as intended, including internal evaluations, audits by an external firm and reviews by each company's board of directors, according to a copy of the one-page accord that Mr. Trump posted to Truth Social . They also agreed to "meet regularly to establish standards and best practices to improve the safety of their systems."
"Over time, it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations," said the accord. "Regardless of whether this is required of companies, we believe that implementing these controls and audits is critical to ensuring a safe future for everyone, and each of our companies are committed to doing this."
Mr. Trump said the AI leaders also discussed forming a 10-person committee to "watch over the enterprise." And the president said he plans to name an "AI czar" in the next three or four days.
Also on Tuesday, the president signed an executive order directing the federal government to use the term "Super Intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence.
The rare meeting between competing tech titans followed months of growing concern from researchers, politicians and industry figures that ever-more-powerful AI technology could pose safety risks.
Both OpenAI and Anthropic have reported instances of their AI models going rogue and gaining unauthorized access to other companies' systems, or being used for dangerous purposes. And Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both companies, publicly warned earlier this month that AI "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He argued AI systems could gain sweeping power over the physical world and become capable of improving themselves without human input.
Some industry leaders, including executives at Anthropic and OpenAI, have called for a slowdown in AI development to better manage the risk. But other figures, like Nvidia's Jensen Huang, have argued some of the warnings are overblown.
Huang said Tuesday that "there's no conflict between innovation, technology and safety," arguing that tech companies are developing stronger AI safety technology as they improve AI's capabilities.
Mr. Trump has not backed stricter AI regulations, instead favoring voluntary safety reviews. He has frequently warned that a nationwide AI slowdown could dent the country's economy and give China's tech industry a chance to catch up.
The president told reporters Tuesday that AI will lead to "unbelievable growth for our country," and if bad actors seek to exploit it, "we're going to be able to nab them." He also said tech companies have an incentive to police themselves and each other because "their companies are at stake."
Beyond the safety worries, there are also mounting concerns about the impact that AI could have on the world — from the potential for large-scale job loss to the rapid development of data centers to support advanced AI models.
As more state and local governments push back on data center development, Mr. Trump said communities that accept the facilities will "greatly benefit financially."
"The data centers are making an absolute fortune. But now, the people are going to benefit directly, whether it's teachers that get paid a bonus, whether it's people that live in the community that get paid a dividend," he told CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes.
But lawmakers who favor more stringent AI regulations may be skeptical of voluntary standards set by the industry. In a statement shortly after Tuesday's meeting, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia called for Congress to pass mandatory testing, evaluation and incident reporting rules for the most advanced AI models.
"The companies building the most powerful AI systems are warning us that the technology is advancing faster than our safeguards," Warner said. "The president's response? To rename it and tell the companies developing it to regulate themselves."

The supreme court has allowed the Trump administration to resume deporting people to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, bolstering a tool Donald Trump has used for rapid expulsions as part of ⁠his immigration crackdown.
The justices granted the DOJ’s request to halt ​Boston-based US district judge Brian Murphy’s ruling that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful , while the administration appeals the matter to the supreme court. They also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December, with a ⁠formal ruling on policy to follow.
Its three liberal justices dissented from the decision.
Federal attorneys said the lower-court decision forced the cancellation of a deportation flight carrying about 70 people bound for three countries.
The justices previously allowed the deportation flights, a core Trump administration policy, to temporarily continue when the case came before them last year. In another win for the administration, the supreme court subsequently lifted limits the judge had imposed to protect a group of men from being sent to South Sudan .
More than 25,000 people have been deported to 29 countries under ⁠the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups, with the vast majority going to Mexico .
The administration has also carried out third-country deportations to politically unstable South Sudan , which the US state department urges Americans to avoid due ​to the risks of crime, kidnapping and armed conflict, as well as Uganda , Equatorial Guinea , ‌ Liberia , the Central African Republic , and other nations.
Senator Chris Van Hollen has released a statement in response to the Senate’s vote failing to pass his resolution requiring the state department report on increasing violence in the West Bank:
“The U.S. Government – including this Administration – has said time and again that our number one priority abroad is ensuring the safety and security of American citizens. And yet, as we’ve seen violence rise in the West Bank, nine American citizens have been killed in recent years, and they have received no justice and no accountability. Their families – and the American people – deserve answers on their deaths. But today Republicans denied them that. Meanwhile, the Palestinian people have also borne the toll of this violence day in and day out. They too deserve justice and accountability. But again, Republicans blocked that today. While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more. It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of U.S. taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.”

“The terminology used by the Federal Government should reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people,” the order reads. “Accordingly, the term ‘Super Intelligence’ more appropriately captures the promise, potential, and rapidly advancing capabilities of these technologies.”
The order directs “executive departments and agencies to use the term in “official correspondence, public communications, websites, reports, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents within the executive branch.”

The Transportation Security Administration confirmed the decision in a statement: This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and ​our commitment to hospitality by having ‌these officers on ‌their feet and alert. All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to ‌be capable of performing their vital national security function.“
The TSA workers’ union, the ⁠American Federation ​of Government Employees TSA Council 100, criticzed the move, saying it showed “disregard for workers’ rights and ⁠safety” and that the chairs TSA workers used while checking IDs “serve as basic ergonomic and safety support for officers that stand and walk on hard surfaces all ⁠day.”
Legal immigration from 45 Muslim-majority countries fell 96% since 2024, according to a new analysis from the Cato Institute, a libertarian thinktank. The White House’s “Rapid Response” account shared the analysis in a social media post today.
“During his campaign in 2016, President Trump repeatedly proposed an outright ban on Muslims entering the United States. He then claimed that this policy idea morphed into the travel ban to avoid potential constitutional problems,” the report states. “During his 2024 campaign, he said he would bring back an even stricter ban than the one in his first term. He has succeeded.”
Citing state department data, the Cato report states that, “ Monthly immigrant visa issuances and permanent lawful refugee admissions fell from 21,096 in December 2024 to 808 in February 2026.”
Last week, CNN reported that the Trump administration plans to accept 17,500 refugees in fiscal year 2027, the vast majority of them white South Africans, citing a copy of the report to Congress. Earlier this year, the administration raised the cap for South African refugees, setting a limit of 17,500 refugees from the country.
“The United States anticipates that Afrikaners from South Africa will fully assimilate into the United States in a manner that preserves taxpayer resources for U.S. citizens and does not anticipate other countries resettling Afrikaners,” the report states.

While the decision does not change anything about Carroll’s receipt of the payout, its revelation effectively means that Trump will no longer oppose the monetary outcome he had long fought.
This decision was revealed Tuesday by the United States court of appeals for the second circuit.

In a social media post, the California Democrat added, “Trump let Xi walk away without a binding treaty on AI. And now he’s doing free PR for AI CEOs,” referring to the meetings Trump has held with Chinese president Xi Jinping and tech company executives this week.

articles.title_zh: Andy Burnham to fight next election on pledge to change voting system
articles.content_orig:
By GREG HEFFER, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 10:03 EDT, 29 September 2026 | Updated: 12:39 EDT, 29 September 2026
Andy Burnham today vowed to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections.
In his first Labour conference speech as Prime Minister, Mr Burnham promised to introduce a 'new politics' through electoral reform.
He confirmed he would fight the next General Election, scheduled for 2029, with a Labour manifesto commitment to alter the system for choosing UK governments.
The PM, a long-time supporter of proportional representation, said a change would ensure 'everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard'.
Mr Burnham announced the creation of a new 'national commission' for electoral reform and invited rival political parties to be part of its work.
Changing the first-past-the-post system to proportional representation could allow smaller parties – including the Greens – to form part of a Westminster government.
Mr Burnham's plans are likely to revive warnings of a 'coalition of chaos' – made up of a variety of Left-wing or nationalist parties – taking charge of Britain.
But in his conference speech in Liverpool, the PM suggested it was the current first-past-the-post system that was to blame for the country's recent churn of premiers.
Andy Burnham today set out his intent to scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system for Westminster elections
He argued that Britain should not be governed by a 'divisive' administration elected with '30 per cent of the vote or less'.
Just ten weeks on from his brutal ousting of Sir Keir Starmer as PM, Mr Burnham told Labour members there was a need to change the country's politics.
He said: 'Westminster prizes point-scoring over problem-solving. And that is why so many things go unfixed for so long.
'If we want to change Britain, we need to change ourselves. I will work as hard as I can to get as much cross-party support for our plan for Britain as I can.
'If we can secure that, it will project a message of confidence and stability to the markets and the world about Britain's future direction.'
The PM has so far refused to call a snap General Election in order to win his own mandate from the country.
This is despite him having called for the Tories to do exactly that when they changed leaders while in power.
But he used his first Labour conference speech as PM to demand a 'new politics', as he bowed to calls from his party's MPs for a national commission on electoral reform.
Mr Burnham added: 'We can't succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times.
'It is always in my mind that I'm the seventh PM in ten years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.
'We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No10 to a divisive government on 30 per cent of the vote or less.
'Conference, in past years you have voted twice to support electoral reform.
'I hear you, I agree with you and today I am announcing a new national commission on electoral reform.
'I invite all political parties to be a part of its work.
'We will contest the next election with a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system so everyone's vote counts and everyone's voice is heard.'
However, immediately after Mr Burnham's speech, senior Labour figures questioned his desire to pursue a change to the UK's voting system.
Asked if there were any elements of the speech she may not have agreed on, skills minister Jacqui Smith, said: 'Electoral reform isn't top of my list of priorities.
'Good luck to the commission. I shall be interested with what it comes out with.
'But you know, respect to Andy, he has also long argued for that – it is something that has got a lot of support in the hall, probably a considerable amount of support in the country, and fair enough to him for trying to find a way through it.'
Former Northern Ireland secretary Hilary Benn described Mr Burnham's address as an 'inspirational speech' but also suggested he was unsure about electoral reform.
'We'll see what the commission on electoral reform produces,' he said.
Labour's party conference voted to support moving towards a proportional representation voting system in 2022.
But the party's 2024 manifesto instead focused its electoral and constitutional changes on extending voting to 16 and 17-year-olds and House of Lords reform.
Mr Burnham has previously spoken of how his late father Roy – who died earlier this month after suffering with Alzheimer's – was unaware that his son had swung behind one of his political passions, a change in the voting system to proportional representation.
'I don't think he's ever realised, because of his condition, that I've come round to PR, which is one of his missions – to get me to accept that,' the PM told The Times in July.

articles.title_orig: China pressure accelerates Philippines-Taiwan ties, analysts say
articles.title_zh: China pressure accelerates Philippines-Taiwan ties, analysts say
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan’s plan to open a second trade office in the Philippines is an example of Manila and Taipei accelerating cooperation in response to Chinese pressure in the South China Sea, analysts told Radio Free Asia.
During a radio interview on Sept. 15, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said that Taipei’s plan to open a second representative office in Cebu, the Philippines’ second largest city, was going smoothly.
Taipei’s trade offices serve as de facto embassies and consulates in countries that officially recognize China, but maintain unofficial relations with Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be a rogue province.
Foreign Minister Lin said that the additional trade office would serve travelers and businesses in the central Philippines, and would be an integral part of a proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor.
Days later, Taiwan confirmed that it had donated a decommissioned patrol vessel to the Philippines for use in its coast guard.
These developments are directly related to Beijing’s hostile tactics in the South China Sea, Ray Powell, executive director of Stanford University’s SeaLight maritime transparency project, told RFA. Beijing claims the entirety of the sea as its territory, including the area within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, which Manila calls the West Philippine Sea.
“Of course China’s aggression in the West Philippine Sea is a central part of this story,” said Powell. “It has made Manila less willing to grant Beijing the kind of deference that other countries like Malaysia or Papua New Guinea have recently been so eager to show on Taiwan policy.”
Papua New Guinea announced in July that it would close the Taiwan trade office in Port Moresby, and Malaysia’s Prime Minister Ibrahim Anwar in August controversially stated in an interview with Al Jazeera that he sees “Taiwan as part of China, period.”
The trend of smaller countries showing deference to China “has conditioned Beijing to expect that its coercive methods will always produce compliance eventually,” Powell said. “For now at least it has not produced that kind of result in the Philippines.”
As a condition of entering into official relations with China, countries must affirm that there is one China and recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China.
China’s official stance, the one-China principle, states that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. Many countries maintain their own one-China policies that stop short of the principle to allow unofficial ties with Taipei.
When Taiwan announced the plan to open a new trade office in Cebu, Beijing protested, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urging the Philippines to uphold the one-China Principle through “concrete actions” and refrain from taking steps that could damage relations with China.
“No matter how the DPP authorities collude with external forces or in what form they seek so-called ‘diplomatic breakthroughs,’ their efforts to serve the goal of ‘Taiwan independence’ are doomed to be futile,” Guo said, referring to Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party.
The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs responded that Manila’s one-China policy remained unchanged but did not prevent economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan.
Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. was more direct, telling local media: “We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them.”
The exchange highlights a widening difference between Manila and Beijing over what the Philippines’ one-China policy allows.
The Taiwan trade office in Cebu should not be interpreted as a change in Manila’s formal position, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA.
“Rather, I think it reflects the ongoing expansion and institutionalization of the Philippines’ unofficial and functional relationship with Taiwan,” he said. “This distinction is important: Manila continues to recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China under its one-China Policy, yet it does not view this policy as precluding economic, cultural, or other practical forms of engagement with Taiwan.”
That relationship had already begun expanding before the latest dispute.
In April 2025, Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration relaxed decades-old restrictions on engagement with Taiwan. Most Philippine officials may now travel there for economic, trade and investment purposes if they use ordinary passports and do not use their official titles.
The restrictions continue to apply to the president, vice president, foreign secretary and defense secretary, illustrating the line Manila is trying to maintain between functional engagement and steps that might resemble formal diplomatic recognition.
“Currently, Manila appears intent on maintaining a distinction between expanding functional ties and taking actions that could be construed as formal diplomatic recognition,” Kristanto said. “The 2025 guidelines are particularly illustrative: they facilitate interactions with Taiwan for economic and investment purposes while retaining restrictions on contacts involving the Philippines’ most senior officials.”
Practical interests are also driving the relationship. More than 200,000 Filipinos work in Taiwan, and the two sides offer visa-free entry to each other’s citizens. Taipei has also placed greater emphasis on trade, investment, tourism and supply-chain cooperation with the Philippines.
Foreign Minister Lin said the proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor would connect with the U.S.-Japan-Philippines-backed Luzon Economic Corridor, an initiative aimed at strengthening infrastructure and supply chains.
Kristanto cautioned against explaining the closer relationship entirely through the South China Sea dispute.
“The deterioration in Manila-Beijing relations has certainly made Taiwan more strategically relevant to the Philippines, and we have seen indications of expanding practical cooperation in areas such as maritime security,” he said.
“But many drivers of closer Philippines-Taiwan relations – economic links, labor, geographical proximity, and supply-chain cooperation – exist independently of the South China Sea dispute. I therefore see pressure from China more as an accelerant to an existing trend than as its sole cause.”
Powell said the Philippines increasingly viewed China’s treatment of Taiwan as part of a wider effort to pressure smaller countries that resisted Beijing’s preferred regional order.
“There’s an active attempt by China, very obvious now, to make a more Sinocentric world and to put down others who do not agree with them – particularly when these others are smaller countries,” Powell said, quoting from a recent SeaLight podcast interview with Teodoro.
Kristanto said the significance of the Cebu office lay less in the facility itself than in Manila’s growing confidence in defining its relationship with Taipei on its own terms.
“Manila appears increasingly willing to insist that maintaining a one-China policy does not give Beijing a veto over its unofficial relationship with Taiwan,” Kristanto said.
“So, in my view, the significance of the Cebu office lies less in the office itself than in what it tells us about how much more comfortable Manila has become in expanding ties with Taiwan while arguing that its formal diplomatic position remains unchanged.”

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs CEO succession planning faces one big problem
articles.content_orig:
Goldman Sachs is on top of Wall Street right now, advising on more than $1 trillion in merger deals and generating more than $12 billion in equities revenue in the first six months of the year alone.
Those records make it all the more striking that Goldman's board has reportedly discussed replacing CEO David Solomon, 64, with president John Waldron, 57, as early as next year.
The succession plan, which would elevate Solomon to executive chairman, could be voted on by the bank's board in coming months, The Wall Street Journal reported late Monday.
The transition would be one of the "smoother and more deliberate" leadership handovers seen on Wall Street, Wells Fargo banking analyst Mike Mayo wrote Monday.
But there's a key risk facing Goldman: Solomon may not be ready to give up his seat, and Waldron may not be willing to wait for it indefinitely.
Solomon has gotten Goldman back on track after an ill-fated foray into consumer banking earlier in his tenure. With help from a deals rebound powered by the Trump administration and the artificial intelligence boom, Goldman is once again a clean story for investors: It's the top pure-play investment bank.
"It's just very hard for a person like that to decide they are really going to retire," said retired University of Delaware law professor Charles Elson . "Being 65 years old today is like being 55 was 30 years ago."
Elson also noted that Solomon is chairman of Goldman's board and holds outsized influence over the body, making it hard for him to be forced out.
Goldman spokesman Tony Fratto said there is "no definitive timeline for succession" at the bank. Bank boards often discuss succession planning over the near, medium and longer term.
Another expert in CEO succession, Yale School of Management's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, said it would be bad governance if Goldman's board was trying to "drive out a high performing CEO like David Solomon."
Under Solomon, who took over as CEO in 2018, Goldman shares are up more than 300%, the second-best performance versus the KBW Bank Index , according to Mayo. Only JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon , who has led his firm for nearly 21 years, has done better.
That leaves Goldman in something of a bind: Even if Solomon is planning on leaving in a year, he has little incentive to say so. Doing so would make him a lame duck with less influence inside the bank, according to Elson.
But if Solomon decides he wants to remain CEO amid an AI boom that he believes is in its early innings, Waldron may tire of waiting for the crown.
After all, Waldron, Goldman's president and chief operating officer, had reportedly been in discussions for leadership roles at alternative asset managers Apollo and Carlyle .
To keep him, Goldman gave Waldron an $80 million retention package that lasts through 2030. Even then, a deep-pocketed suitor could make a play for Waldron, said Elson.
"There will always be tension in a set up like that," Elson said. "It's like Prince Charles waiting for his mother to die. You can't set your own priorities, because there's someone else in charge."

articles.title_orig: New York judge orders city to scrap Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax rollout
articles.title_zh: New York judge orders city to scrap Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax rollout
articles.content_orig:
New York City’s planned tax on secondary homes was dealt a major setback Tuesday after a Staten Island judge ruled in favor of the plaintiffs challenging the rollout.
The pied-à-terre tax, which places a surcharge on non-primary residences in New York City valued over $5 million, as well as co-ops valued at $1 million or more, was rolled out as part of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s 2027 fiscal year budget in an attempt to close the city’s budget gap. Gov. Kathy Hochul had backed the idea.
Mamdani, who took office in January, promised to “govern as a democratic socialist” and campaigned on plans to make the city more affordable and improve New Yorkers’ daily lives. In his first few months in office, he delivered a rent freeze for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments across the city.
The plaintiffs in the lawsuit did not challenge the legality of the tax itself, but rather the rollout. Three petitioners alleged the city had incorrectly “identified their homes as potentially subject to the surcharge,” despite being their primary residences.
New York City homeowners file lawsuit challenging rollout of Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax
The city’s Department of Finance website posted a tax roll in July that included names and addresses of over 900,000 New York City homeowners, even if they were not subject to the tax.
Judge Wayne M. Ozzi of Richmond County ruled the roll must be removed from the website, but can be replaced with a secondary roll “reflecting those properties actually subject to the surcharge.”
Approximately 17,000 notices were also mailed to residents at the start of the process, which notified them that they would need to file for exemption or be subject to the tax. Tuesday’s ruling came one week before the October 6 exemption deadline.
Those previously mailed notices must be canceled as well, Ozzi ruled. New notices can be mailed in compliance with a list of rules, including that they can only be mailed only after “individualized initial determination utilizing any and all resources and information” available to the Department of Finance.
“We’re gratified that the court has recognized we were right all along. The fact is that this administration failed to follow state law when it burdened New York City homeowners with proving they live in their own homes or be on the hook for paying a new surcharge,” Randy Mastro, an attorney representing the plaintiffs, said in a statement following Tuesday’s ruling.
“Now the administration must go back and do what it should have done from the start: use all the information at its disposal to make an individualized ‘initial determination’ about who truly owes this surcharge before demanding that they pay it.”
A spokesperson for Mamdani said in a statement the decision was “wrong.”
“The pied-à-terre surcharge is about a basic principle of fairness: if you can afford a luxury second home in New York City, you can afford to pay your fair share for the schools, streets and parks that make this city work,” Matt Rauschenbach said.
“Our Administration is fighting every day to deliver for working New Yorkers. The ultra-wealthy are fighting in court to avoid paying their fair share. They have filed lawsuit after lawsuit to protect their privilege, and we will not back down.”
The city appealed the ruling Tuesday evening, a city official told CNN, invoking a stay and allowing it to continue with the implementation of the surcharge while the lower court’s order is on pause.
In addition to the plaintiffs’ win in Richmond County, others are still looking to challenge the law’s constitutionality.
Also Tuesday, a group of Suffolk County homeowners and a co-op sued New York State over the pied-à-terre tax, arguing the law “unlawfully discriminates against nonresidents, applies retroactively, and imposes unconstitutional burdens on homeowners and cooperative buildings.”
The lawsuit also expressed concern over the roll and mail notices – that Ozzi ruled must be canceled – arguing the process “created widespread confusion, raised privacy concerns, and improperly shifted the burden onto homeowners to prove eligibility for an exemption.”
This story has been updated with additional information.
CNN’s Gloria Pazmino contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Mozilla Deploys A New-Look Firefox Across Desktop And Mobile
articles.title_zh: Mozilla Deploys A New-Look Firefox Across Desktop And Mobile
articles.content_orig:
The redesigned browser brings back compact mode and adds a theme picker.
Firefox is now looking quite different for most users after Mozilla started rolling out a redesign to everyone across desktop and mobile. The new look may not be too much of a surprise for some, though. Beta testers have been able to check it out through the Nightly version of the browser for the last few months.
Mozilla says it updated Firefox's themes, icons and colors to modernize it in line with features it has added recently, such as a single off switch for generative AI tools . The redesign itself brings more features to Firefox, as well as the return of compact mode, a much-requested option that Mozilla previously nixed. This minimizes how much screen real estate that the toolbar and tabs take up, so you can see more of the website. There's also a theme picker that includes wallpaper options and the ability to organize shortcuts on the New Tab screen.
Privacy settings are said to be easier to find , and Mozilla claimed it hasn't sacrificed performance. It added that the new Firefox doesn't place features like tab groups, split view and vertical tabs front and center, but they're still close at hand for those who want swift access. Moreover, Mozilla said it designed the customization options with accessibility in mind.

The focus of OpenAI’s Dev Day on Tuesday may have been on its agentic assistants known as Dots , or its new AI models , but combined, the AI company’s announcements pointed towards a bigger plan: a disruption of the traditional app store model. Taken together, today’s announcements turn ChatGPT itself into the place where software can be discovered, launched, and used by people and agents alike.
In addition, OpenAI introduced a way for people to bring their ChatGPT identity with them, while also allowing them to use their existing AI allowance in third-party apps.
This isn’t the first time OpenAI has experimented with how apps could operate within its familiar chatbot interface, but the current vision feels more fleshed out than before.
For starters, the company is turning ChatGPT itself into a surface for launching apps. The chatbot, which the company says now has 1.2 billion weekly users, has yet to fully capitalize on its potential as a discovery mechanism for finding and using apps that work with AI.
To change that, ChatGPT will begin to make app suggestions within the flow of conversation when it recognizes that a particular app could help the user complete their task. From there, the user will be able to connect the app and begin using it directly within ChatGPT.
This is also aided by the expansion of ChatGPT’s plugin architecture, which now supports extensions.
This allows app developers to build interactive panels where users can work with their tools while they’re chatting with ChatGPT. This essentially turns the apps and services that users would have previously used via the web or through a native desktop or mobile app into something that’s operated directly within ChatGPT.
Developers that sign on with the system can build AI-native versions of their apps through ChatGPT, the same way they would through the open web or a mobile app store. As more and more discovery happens through AI chat, it’s a distribution channel that’s hard to pass up.
Users get an incentive to use that channel too, because “ Sign in with ChatGPT ” will let them bring their AI allowance with them. (OpenAI has 16 launch partners on this effort, including Cognition’s Devin, Notion, Vercel, T3, OpenClaw, and Dactyl, but plans to add more soon, it says.)
In a demo at OpenAI’s Dev Day event, the company showed off how its own new meeting app could work inside ChatGPT, showing upcoming meetings from the user’s calendar. Here, the user could easily choose to use AI to take meeting notes, then receive a summary of follow-up items when the meeting wrapped.
In another example, users would work with design-focused apps like those from Figma and Adobe to work on revisions of their current project or use a particular feature that would have otherwise required a standalone app.
The apps can be shared with others, like work colleagues, in the lightweight websites ChatGPT now produces. From these ChatGPT sites, a user’s coworkers could sign in to the app with their own credentials and permissions, making the software experience personalized to them.
OpenAI also talked about improvements to how developers submit plugins for review — OpenAI’s version of Apple’s App Review process, if you will. Now, developers will be able to track their review, see what needs to be fixed, request a human review, and update their plugin’s tools without starting their whole submission over.
The company also announced a new enterprise app marketplace where partners can market their services. At launch, there are some 30-plus partners offering their app through the OpenAI Marketplace, including Adobe, Figma, Sierra, Decagon, HubSpot, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Harvey, Legora, Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike, Baseten, and others. Eligible customers can apply part of their OpenAI commitment toward approved partner software, OpenAI said.
Beyond turning ChatGPT into an app discovery tool where users connect with apps directly, OpenAI’s embrace of agents is gently pushing users into a new era where they don’t have to think as much about which app to use or why, relying instead on their AI agents’ suggestions.
With the launch of its autonomous AI agents known as Dots , agents will navigate the web for you, executing the tasks that need to be done in their own cloud infrastructure. Each Dot has its own cloud computer and browser, and can also use connected apps. Compare this to the old model, where users who wanted to manage some type of project — like building a website or coordinating a meeting calendar — would have to download different apps to their computer or phone to make that happen.
Now, users will instead tell an AI agent what they want to have done, and it will simply do it for them. In some cases, the agent’s work may require access to another AI model or a particular application. But this is something the agent may bring to the user, rather than the other way around — where the user is the one to go out and seek the particular tool for the job.
As OpenAI explains, the Dots will be able to connect to its ecosystem of now over 4,000 apps.
What’s more, the Dots can be proactive, perhaps jumping in to offer help with a project or bug, or handling a task the user forgot — but all done with the user’s approval. The Dots will perform what OpenAI calls “proactive research” in the background using connected apps in a read-only mode, but users would still have control over the actions they take.
This system could give app makers another way to reach customers outside of Apple and Google’s app stores. For instance, users could subscribe to a service through the app maker’s website, then connect that account to ChatGPT or Codex for their agent to use. OpenAI has not said, however, that these features would eliminate the need for separate third-party subscriptions or other charges.
Notably, OpenAI didn’t tease any plans on this front today, instead focusing on how it’s building the discovery, distribution, and interface pieces to counter the app store model, along with an identity layer and a mechanism for sharing a user’s existing ChatGPT AI allowance. It did not announce plans Tuesday for a billing or revenue-sharing system that’s comparable to the economic layer of traditional app stores.

A top Federal Reserve official suggested Tuesday that the central bank could wait until December before raising interest rates again, pushing back against market bets on a follow-up increase next month.
The remarks from New York Fed President John Williams carry particular weight because as vice chair of the Fed’s rate-setting committee, he has typically sought to reflect the views of the committee’s center of gravity rather than stake out his own position.
Inflation remains too high, and another rate increase “late this year” might be appropriate, Williams said. But for now, the Fed can likely take time to review additional data before tightening policy further, he said.
“With the policy action we took at our September meeting, there is no need for urgency,” Williams said in a speech in Buffalo, N.Y.

articles.title_orig: Coming to America - pandas and international politics at a zoo
articles.title_zh: Coming to America - pandas and international politics at a zoo
articles.content_orig:
Are panda’s ursine politicians? Well, actually, they’re more like international statesmen.
And some Northeastern University experts believe that a pair of Chinese giant pandas that arrived in the U.S. on Sunday are a sign of soothing tensions between Beijing and Washington.
“Pandas are an unusually effective diplomatic symbol,” said Xiaoxiao Shen , an assistant research professor at Northeastern who focuses on Chinese international politics.
“They are associated with China but aren’t controversial.”
It’s called “soft diplomacy”, said Daniel Aldrich , a Northeastern University professor who teaches political science, describing a diplomatic tool used to show good will to other nations.
Typically it is done by giving food, medicine, other aid – or in this case, pandas –  to help inspire people in foreign countries to feel more favorable to your nation, he said.
“China wants to see happy headlines about pandas and not the abuse of the Uyghurs,” a minority population in China, Aldrich said.
Shen explained that as political tensions rise and fall between the U.S. and China, pandas are given or taken away. There used to be 20 Chinese-owned pandas at American zoos. Since 2024, all but six have gone home, as relations between Beijing and Washington have ebbed and flowed.
“There is a clear political dimension,” Shen said.
The arrival of the pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, at  Zoo Atlanta after their 8,000 mile journey from Chengdu, China, was announced by Chinese president Xi Jinping as he stood beside President Trump at a visit to the White House on Sept. 24.
Xi declared that the bears were an “envoy of friendship.”
The practice of giving bears dates back to the Tang dynasty in the early about 1,500 years ago, at a time when daughters were often given in marriage to foreign kings and nomadic rulers in China to solidify treaties and border disputes, said Mark Henderson , a Northeastern political science professor who teaches at the Oakland campus.
The Bronx zoo received two pandas from China in 1941 and in 1972 the People’s Republic of China gifted then President Richard Nixon and his wife Pat with a pair of pandas, Hsing-Hsing and Ling-Ling, as a gesture of friendship.
Aside from deploying bears as a goodwill gesture, China has been using soft diplomacy to gain favor elsewhere in the world, including in Africa where it has launched vaccination programs and invested heavily in building roads, bridges, ports and other infrastructure, Aldrich said.
A July 2026 Pew Research Center survey of 36 nations found that China is seen more favorably than the U.S. across the globe with countries expressing more confidence in Xi than Trump. Even America’s closest neighbors Canada and Mexico – view China more positively than the U.S., the nonprofit thinktank found.
“There are two ways to influence people around the world,” Aldrich said. “The first is to bomb them. The second is to feed them, give them aid. As we’ve seen in Iran over these last seven months, bombs aren’t working.”
The U.S. had used soft diplomacy to great success in past years. In 1948, America  committed $15 billion to the Marshall Plan to help rebuild Western Europe following World War II. The approach built trust and strong alliances as “America [was] is seen as the friendly nation,” Aldrich said.
But in recent years, the U.S. has all but dismantled the United States Agency for International Development or USAID, a state-run program that in 2023 spent about $40 billion in food, medical and emergency assistance across the globe according to the Congressional Research Service, according to Pew. That aid ended in 2025 when the government functionally dismantled the program.
In addition, the U.S. also cut ties with the World Health Organization, or WHO, in 2025, citing mismanagement and lack of transparency, according to a release from the U.S. Health and Human Services Department.
“People around the world, especially Africa, think that America has abandoned them,” Henderson said, as the lion’s share of USAID went to nations on that continent.
But the pandas coming-to-America moment is a sign of political thawing between the U.S. and China – at least for now, experts said.
“The pandas are given or taken away as China thinks favorably of you or not,” Henderson said.

articles.title_orig: California bans officers’ use of electric-shock gloves after ICE reveals plan to equip agents
articles.title_zh: California bans officers’ use of electric-shock gloves after ICE reveals plan to equip agents
articles.content_orig:
State passes law banning local, state and federal officers from using gloves that deliver painful electric shocks
California has passed a law Tuesday banning local, state and federal law enforcement officers from using gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks to people .
The ban on shock gloves will take effect next year and remain in place until 2030. It comes weeks after US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) moved to equip its officers with the gloves, which are designed to gain compliance from combative individuals. Last month, the agency awarded a nearly $17m contract to buy 6,000 pairs.
“Trump has put his political interests above the health, safety and livelihood of American families,” Gavin Newsom, California’s governor, said in a statement after signing the law. “California is taking action to strengthen transparency, accountability, and oversight around immigration enforcement in our state.”
The law is the latest example of how Democratic-led states have been pushing back against Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts since he took office last year. In California, lawmakers passed at least two dozen bills this year seeking to fortify immigrants’ rights, restrict cooperation with federal immigration agents and tighten regulations on immigrant detention facilities, among other things.
Nationwide, 17 states with Democratic-led legislatures have passed a total of more than 100 pro-immigrant bills this year, according to an Associated Press analysis using the bill tracking software Plural. The most common purpose is to limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement agents.
LaShae Sharp-Collins, a Democratic California assembly member, said she introduced the shock-gloves legislation to “put a pause” on law enforcement’s use of the devices while the state examines their potential risks. The law requires the state’s justice department to study their safety and report to lawmakers by 2029.
“There’s a lot of unrest and a lot of uncertainty,” she said in an interview. “A lot of people are scared.”
The law will again test the state’s authority to restrict federal agents amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. A federal judge earlier this year blocked the state’s first-in-the-nation law barring federal officers from wearing face coverings, deeming it too selective because it applied to local and federal law enforcement but exempted state officers.
Lawmakers passed a new bill this year to make the ban apply to all officers. Newsom signed that legislation.
Kevin Johnson, a professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis School of Law, said courts are likely to ultimately rule that the state cannot bar federal officers from wearing shock gloves or face coverings. The laws are well-intentioned, he said, but likely conflict with the supremacy clause of the US constitution, which generally sets federal law as supreme over conflicting state law.
“The state has very limited, if any, powers in dictating to the federal government how its officers are armed,” he said.
Sacramento sheriff Jim Cooper, a Democrat and former state lawmaker, said banning shock gloves “really makes no sense” because they are among the non-lethal tools officers can use if necessary.
“When the federal government does something, the state legislature wants to ban it,” he said at a news conference. “They’re making our job harder.”
Sharp-Collins said ICE’s plan to use shock gloves was the catalyst for the ban. But she cited their use by other officers, including a case in which a Kentucky family alleged a man died after being tased and shocked with the gloves dozens of times while in law enforcement custody in 2024.
Scott Wiener, a state senator and San Francisco Democrat who wrote last year’s mask ban, also authored this year’s measure to expand it to state officers.
“California must use every available tool to stand up for our communities under attack from ICE’s secret police terror campaign,” he said in a statement after it passed the legislature.

Warner Bros. is asking moviegoers to “decide for yourself” with a new ad for Tom Cruise’s “ Digger ” that touts both negative and positive reactions.
“Masterpiece” and “Unpleasant” are quoted in the same still of the new trailer, which also toggles between the words “Brilliant” and “Baffling” as well as “Magnificent” and “Insufferable.” These quotes are from film influencers who screened the movie early and posted their reactions after the social embargo lifted on Sept. 22.
“Same film, different truth,” reads the ad for “Digger,” which stars Cruise as an oil tycoon whose drilling triggers a climate crisis. The film, from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu, marks Cruise’s first non-action hero role in nearly a decade.
Warner Bros. posted the new ad an hour before the review embargo, which is when film critics were allowed to publish their reviews. The “decide for yourself” campaign may have been an attempt to get ahead of the critics, who were, as a whole, far less generous than the first wave of social media pundits.
Variety ‘s Owen Gleiberman called the film “so full of itself” in his review , writing, “The movie cost north of $125 million to make, and that figure is not only too big to probably justify itself; it’s a testament to the arrogance of the filmmakers — to the assumption that we’ll turn out in droves for this ponderous absurdist lecture.”
Bilge Ebiri of Vulture wrote in his review, “‘Digger’ is a torturous experience, sometimes purposefully so, often unintentionally so.” And David Ehrlich of IndieWire dubbed it a “surreal misfire,” giving the movie a C+ grade. (“Digger” currently sits at a 52% score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes.)
Of course, those are just critics’ opinions, so for those waiting to decide for themselves, “Digger” premieres in theaters on Oct. 2.

articles.title_orig: Two Indian nationals charged with smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China: DOJ
articles.title_zh: Two Indian nationals charged with smuggling counterfeit Ozempic from China: DOJ
articles.content_orig:
Two Indian nationals have been charged in federal court in Florida with an alleged conspiracy to smuggle counterfeit Ozempic from China in a scheme that purportedly continued even after the Food and Drug Administration seized some of the fake weight-loss drugs in 2023 and warned the public about it, the Department of Justice said Tuesday.
One of the men, 33-year-old Swapnadip Roy, was extradited from Italy and made his initial appearance in U.S. District Court in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday.
Roy and his alleged co-conspirator, Vicky Ramancha, 37, are charged in an indictment with one count of conspiracy to commit smuggling and to defraud the U.S., three counts of smuggling, and two counts of selling counterfeit drugs and holding counterfeit drugs for sale. If convicted, they both face a maximum sentence of 71 years in prison.
Ramancha remains at large.
Court documents state Roy and Ramancha, starting in July 2023 and continuing to the following April, allegedly obtained counterfeit Ozempic from unauthorized sources in China. The popular drug is made by Novo , which recently rebranded from its name Novo Nordisk.
The material they and their co-conspirators allegedly distributed "included counterfeit packaging, package inserts, pen labels, and needles meant to deceive downstream customers into believing they were purchasing authentic Ozempic authorized by the manufacturer," DOJ said.
The newly unsealed indictment says that in July 2023, Ramancha executed a sales and purchase agreement with an unidentified company in Lakeland, Florida, agreeing to supply that company with a product described as being Ozempic "at deeply discounted pricing."
A month later, Ramancha executed another agreement with a company in Sanford, Florida, to supply it with a product described as "Ozempic syringes" at deeply discounted pricing, the indictment alleges.
in November 2023, "Roy utilized threats to facilitate the distribution of product in the United States," writing, "Listen i am not your friend okay? I am not that guy," the indictment alleges.
Roy continued, "I am the guy that will cut some one [expletive] head off and [expletive] peoples dead wives corpse with it," the indictment alleges. "You [expletive] up Solve the [expletive] problem. Get the truck over there today."
After Roy and Ramancha learned that the FDA had seized some of their product that they had distributed in the U.S., a co-conspirator asked Ramancha whether the related FDA warning would affect a pending order to 60,000 additional units of Ozempic, the indictment says.
"Ramancha replied, 'Not at all. But you have to make sure your client are not being idiotic,'" the indictment alleges.
The case comes as the use of so-called GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic for weight loss has become increasingly popular in the U.S.
In July, Gallup reported that the percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes rose to 11% in  2026, compared to 3% in 2024.
"And 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, an increase of nine percentage points" over 2024, Gallup noted.
"Counterfeit prescription drugs — especially common ones — threaten the health and safety of every American who depends on the integrity of our pharmaceutical supply," Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the DOJ's Criminal Division said in a statement Tuesday.
"These defendants allegedly exploited people's health to pay themselves. We will keep pursuing anyone who seeks to deceive American consumers with counterfeit drugs," Duva said.

This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
LONDON — A surprise decision by U.K. counterterrorism police to release five suspects on bail during an investigation into a suspected bomb plot at a U.S.-operated air force base in England has deepened questions and uncertainty about the incident.
Police confirmed Tuesday that no explosives were found in three vans linked to the suspects, and said the decision to grant bail was grounded in “experience and strategy.”
President Trump told reporters Monday that he was surprised the five young British men who were arrested Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses near the RAF Fairford base were freed a day later.
“I wouldn’t have done that,” Trump said.
The base has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including this year’s war with Iran. Counterterrorism detectives have said they were investigating “multiple lines of inquiry,” including whether the suspects had a link to Iran. The Islamic Republic has denied involvement.
The head of U.K. Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, stressed that the suspects — all British nationals in their 20s — face stringent conditions and “absolutely remain under investigation.”
“Now, I understand why this development was surprising to some, but I would like to reiterate that this is an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and strategy,” he said.
Taylor said people’s concerns about the incident were being “heightened by the international commentary that we are seeing.”
In an interview with Fox News, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the case “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor” but did not name a specific country or give more details.
“I know a lot of people are disturbed by the news that some of these people have been released on bail, as some of the people are being investigated,” he added.
A police cordon remained in place around three vans found close to the Fairford base on Tuesday, as armed police and counterterrorism officers continued to examine the scene.
A local farmer said she called police after seeing the vans blocking a road near the air base as she drove home in the early hours of Sunday. She said that she came across a group of men, some with their faces covered, nearby, and that the men ran away when they saw her vehicle.
Earlier, army bomb-disposal experts used a robot to examine the vans. Taylor said “a quantity of petrol was recovered” from the vans, but no explosives.
Taylor, the counterterrorism police chief, said lines of inquiry include whether the suspected offenses were committed by “proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”
Investigators haven’t concluded whether the incident was state-backed or what the motive was, but authorities have strongly hinted that Iran is possibly involved. They are also investigating a possible link to Russia or nonstate militant groups. RAF Fairford has also been the focus of protests by anti-war campaigners.
Defense Secretary Wes Streeting said the U.K. “shouldn’t be cowed by saber-rattling from Iran,” adding that “the Iranian regime is one that wishes harm to our country, our allies, and the freedom and democracy that we enjoy.”
The Iranian Embassy denied the country’s involvement in the suspected plot.
Iran and allied militant groups have been accused of plotting or carrying out attacks on U.S., British and Jewish targets in the past, allegedly acting through local proxies while denying responsibility.
The air base houses the headquarters of the U.S. Air Force’s 501st Combat Support Wing and is a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command. Fairford was used during the 1990 Persian Gulf War, the 2003 Iraq war and the U.S.-Israeli bombardment of Iran this year.
British officials have said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased by 50% in the six months to December 2025.
It was unclear whether the arrested men had been on the security services’ radars. Residents described seeing heightened security around RAF Fairford in recent days, with heavy vehicles parked across entrance gates.
Trump said the suspects were detained after cooperation between the U.S. and Britain, and had been “under view” for some time. Police, however, said the arrests were triggered by a late-night call about the suspicious vehicles near the base.
The farmer who called the police, who didn’t want to be named, alleged that her call to police may have foiled the suspected plot. She added that several hours passed between her call and when police “suddenly decided to evacuate people” in the area.
“But meanwhile, those vans were right in the middle of the village next to everyone’s houses and no one did anything,” she said.
Streeting, the defense secretary, said Monday that the farmer had only a “partial picture” of the operation.
Local lawmaker Roz Savage said there was “anger and anxiety” from residents, especially those who were evacuated from their homes and still haven’t been able to return.
“I have so many questions right now, more questions than answers,” she said in a video message on X. “This should not have been allowed to happen.”
Hui and Grant write for the Associated Press. Grant reported from Fairford.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI’s Dots Are Always-On AI Agents—and Its Answer to Meta’s Muse
articles.title_zh: OpenAI’s Dots Are Always-On AI Agents—and Its Answer to Meta’s Muse
articles.content_orig:
Dots are OpenAI’s new always-on AI agents , announced at the company’s DevDay 2026 event on Tuesday in San Francisco. These agents complete tasks on a user’s behalf and are depicted as cute blobs you can personalize and assign multistep projects to complete.
OpenAI’s Dots are powered by the startup’s GPT-6 Astra model . A core selling point is their “always-on” design—unlike a single-turn chatbot experience, these agents constantly crawl the web and attempt to complete whatever task you assign to them. Dots also pull context from connected apps and learn more about your preferences over time.
In one demo example shared by OpenAI, a user’s Dot helps plan dinner. The Dot proactively saw that the user’s calendar showed they were working through dinner and messaged with two GrubHub food delivery options with pricing for each. The user followed up with their food pick and when they wanted it ordered. In another example, a user collaborated with the agent to launch a new website.
Users can message Dots through ChatGPT , Slack, and Microsoft Teams, with the user’s context shared with Dots across modes. In addition, Pro users can join a waitlist to text with their Dots in iMessage or RCS messaging on Android .
The Dots rollout starts today for subscribers to ChatGPT’s Pro tier that costs $100 a month. OpenAI often launches new features first for this higher subscription tier and then rolls them out to a larger subset of users over time. Users can start by controlling one Dot, but the company is expected to eventually roll out the ability to control multiple agents at the same time.
The Dots launch is also part of OpenAI doubling down on its efforts to attract more enterprise clients. On stage at DevDay, CEO Sam Altman announced “specialist Dots” for enterprise customers tuned for specific tasks, like accounting, email marketing, and legal analysis. It adds to the trend of AI agent coworkers being integrated into more professional workflows.
Dots are designed to get explicit approval before taking more sensitive actions on a user's behalf, like installing software or changing a password. Users can enable a Custom Rules tool to set explicit boundaries that they don't want agents to cross, as well as tasks that need more direct permission to complete.
As users connect their data and use agents, it's worth keeping potential security and privacy risks top of mind. OpenAI built safety guardrails into these Dots, but even so, asking agents to automate aspects of your life involves trusting the tools won’t accidentally share information you didn’t intend or get tricked by an online adversary into taking actions you didn’t want. Exercise caution when interacting with this nascent software and connecting data from your pre-existing apps. Also, if your OpenAI account is set to allow model training on your data, this setting carries over to your interactions with the agents.
Personal agents are currently having a breakthrough moment. While this year started with early adopters in Silicon Valley latching onto tools like OpenClaw , the recent release of Meta’s Muse agent reached a larger user base that is now experimenting with personalized agents. Muse rocketed to the top of smartphone app download charts, but Dots has come for Meta's lunch.

articles.title_orig: Boeing’s Starliner Faces a Critical Test This Year as NASA Runs Out of Options
articles.title_zh: Boeing’s Starliner Faces a Critical Test This Year as NASA Runs Out of Options
articles.content_orig:
Months after NASA’s leadership issued a scathing indictment of Boeing’s Starliner capsule — saying the botched 2024 test flight that left two astronauts in space months longer than expected was a disaster in league with Columbia and Challenger — the space agency has revealed a new road map to get Starliner on track for regular flights.
The agency has indicated for some time that Starliner’s next flight would be uncrewed, and NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said Monday that the mission will take place no earlier than December. If that goes well, the earliest Starliner could fly its next crew mission is mid-2028, officials said.
“ Before crewed operations resume,” Isaacman said, some thrusters require “a design modification.”
Starliner will also need a new ride to orbit, as the Atlas rockets that have carried it to space in the past are soon retiring. NASA said Monday the agency is working with Boeing and Atlas provider United Launch Alliance to certify its new Vulcan Centaur rockets for crewed missions as a replacement.
NASA is expecting to pay an additional $359 million for Starliner’s upgrades and Vulcan certification, the agency said Monday.
Monday’s news conference marked the first substantial update about the Boeing Starliner program in months. And it comes as NASA is looking to fill out a long schedule of missions to the International Space Station, which is slated to be decommissioned in the early 2030s but requires a rotating crew of astronauts to maintain operations while in orbit.
Currently, SpaceX’s Crew Dragon capsule is the only operational US vehicle capable of carrying astronauts to and from the orbiting outpost. NASA was nearing the end of its contract with SpaceX for those flights before purchasing three additional missions for $946 million earlier this month.
But SpaceX has made clear it intends to retire its Dragon spacecraft program as it shifts focus to Starship, the gargantuan launch vehicle that aims to send humans to the moon and Mars.
“I do not think it’s a secret that SpaceX intends to sunset older platforms like Falcon and Dragon as they concentrate on their next generation capability, Starship,” Isaacman said Monday. “Given our extensive history with Starliner and the taxpayer investment already made, we believe it represents the fastest path to preserving reliable crewed access to low Earth orbit.”
SpaceX president and chief operating officer Gwynne Shotwell previously acknowledged that Dragon would be discontinued, saying in 2024 that she expects Dragon will cease operations sometime in the 2030s.
It’s not clear whether SpaceX would move to retire Dragon if NASA still needed service flights to the ISS.
But when asked about the matter recently, Shotwell was blunt: “Boeing has been paid — I think probably more than we have been paid — to develop their human capsule,” she said at the All-In Summit earlier this month.
SpaceX has been awarded $5.92 billion in NASA contracts for a demo mission and 17 operational flights, while Boeing has been given $4.82 billion with a mandatory order for just four flights, not including the additional $359 million for the Starliner program revealed Monday. (Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, said Monday the space agency is also reopening the possibility of requiring two additional flights from Boeing under its current contract.)
“We’re just going to let them have some business,” Shotwell said of Boeing.
Starliner has been under development for more than a decade, and problems with the vehicle’s thrusters have plagued its development. Issues cropped up during uncrewed test flights and NASA’s inaugural Boeing Crew Flight Test in June 2024, which included astronauts Suni Williams and Butch Wilmore.
Starliner ran into problems shortly after reaching orbit on that mission. Wilmore and Williams were expected to fly the spacecraft to the ISS and dock for about a week before returning home.
Those plans were quickly dashed, however, when the Starliner spacecraft experienced helium leaks and thruster outages en route to the orbiting laboratory. Ultimately, NASA determined the spacecraft was not safe enough to return Williams and Wilmore home, and they became part of the next space station crew rotation, eventually returning home on a SpaceX capsule. The astronauts ultimately spent more than nine months in orbit.
Isaacman announced Monday that NASA astronaut Woody Hoburg will command the next crewed Starliner mission. Hoburg mentioned Williams and Wilmore’s ordeal at the news conference, saying the astronauts “conducted themselves with the utmost of professionalism, competence, and humility throughout the mission. They are American heroes, and I am deeply humbled to follow in their footsteps.”
Hoburg added that what “keeps me up at night” is not issues with Starliner’s hardware.
“It’s the underlying pattern,” Hoburg said. “It was inadequate systems engineering and integration, creating gaps in hardware qualification. In the case of the helium leaks and the crew module (thruster) failures, the unqualified environment was actually on the ground.”
It’s now clear that Starliner’s thrusters were damaged before ever launching, he said, and the issue should have been caught and prevented before the vehicle got to the launchpad.
During the Starliner test flight, NASA and Boeing insisted the astronauts’ lives were never in danger. But recently Isaacman, who took over the agency in December, moved to classify the botched test flight as a “Type A mishap.” That’s a designation that NASA defines as an incident that results in more than $2 million of damage, the loss of control or destruction of a vehicle, or a loss of life.
The Columbia and Challenger Space Shuttle disasters were also classified as “Type A” incidents.
